title: Machine Learning
teaser: Design and evaluate a supervised prediction system from decision contract to monitored policy.
audience: Adult learners evaluating or building prediction systems

sourceCredits.title: Machine Learning: Applied Supervised Learning primer
sourceCredits.author: lrnki project
sourceCredits.note: Accepted as a local authoring basis without independent external fact verification.

legs.title: Make the whole prediction system evaluable

stops.label: Frame the prediction at decision time

sections.title: An operational question comes before the model
sections.body: Define one prediction unit, the exact prediction time, the target and its horizon, the features available by that cutoff, and the decision the output will influence. A field that appears in the historical database is not automatically usable: if it arrives after the decision, it violates the availability contract. Choose evaluation measures around the consequences and capacity of the real decision, then compare with a credible non-ML baseline.

sourceAnchor.heading: 1. Frame the Prediction Problem Around a Decision
sourceAnchor.quote: A supervised-learning project begins with an operational question, not a model family.

activities.prompt: At order review time, a system predicts whether an order will be returned. Which candidate feature clearly violates the availability contract?

options.text: The final return resolution recorded two weeks after the order
The basket value visible when review begins
The account age calculated at the review cutoff
The shipping method selected before review

explanation.text: The final resolution is caused by events after the prediction cutoff and cannot exist at review time. Historical co-location does not make future information available to the deployed system.

sourceAnchor.heading: 1. Frame the Prediction Problem Around a Decision
sourceAnchor.quote: Features must be available at the exact moment a prediction would be made.

activities.prompt: Match each contract element to the question it settles.

pairs.right: What one row represents at inference
How far after the cutoff the target is observed
What action will use the output

explanation.text: The unit names each prediction case, the horizon bounds its future outcome, and the decision determines which errors, output form, and capacity constraints matter.

sourceAnchor.heading: 1. Frame the Prediction Problem Around a Decision
sourceAnchor.quote: The prediction unit identifies one row at inference time: an account-month, a component-cycle, a patient-visit, or a document.

stops.label: Keep evaluation information out of fitting

sections.title: A split must imitate how new predictions arrive
sections.body: Estimate generalization on observations that did not choose the fitted system. Split by entity, time, site, or another grouping when rows share information; random rows are appropriate only for the matching deployment claim. Fit preprocessing inside each training partition, and keep held-out data from influencing feature choices, thresholds, or transformations. Target leakage includes any predictor containing the target or later consequences unavailable at prediction time. Reusing test results for another design iteration quietly turns the test set into validation data.

sourceAnchor.heading: 2. Splits, Evaluation Protocols, and Leakage
sourceAnchor.quote: Generalization performance must be estimated on observations not used to choose the fitted system.

activities.prompt: A service predicts next-month cancellation from monthly account histories. Which evaluation most closely tests future deployment?

options.text: Train on earlier months and test on later mature outcomes, keeping each cutoff's future fields unavailable
Randomly mix all account-months, including later history from the same accounts
Fit preprocessing on all months before making the split
Tune repeatedly until the final test month gives the preferred score

explanation.text: A time-ordered evaluation preserves the direction of information and tests later cases. Mixing histories, fitting transformations globally, or adapting to test results lets evaluation information influence development.

sourceAnchor.heading: 2. Splits, Evaluation Protocols, and Leakage
sourceAnchor.quote: Time-ordered prediction normally requires a temporal evaluation: train on earlier data and evaluate on later data.

activities.prompt: Two practices preserve an evaluation boundary. One contaminates it. Find the impostor.

statements.text: Keep rows from the same entity together when identity-specific history could leak across the split.
Fit learned preprocessing separately inside each training fold.
After reading the test score, retune the threshold and still call that score a final untouched estimate.

explanation.text: Once a test result drives another design choice, that test has participated in selection. It is now validation evidence, not an untouched final estimate.

sourceAnchor.heading: 2. Splits, Evaluation Protocols, and Leakage
sourceAnchor.quote: If test results influence another design iteration, the test set has become validation data;

stops.label: Turn scores into a monitored policy

sections.title: A useful score still needs a decision rule
sections.body: Ranking, probability quality, and decision value are different properties. Calibration asks whether cases assigned probability near p experience the event about fraction p in the relevant population. Choose thresholds or top-k policies from benefits, costs, capacity, and subgroup behavior, using held-out data. After deployment, monitor service health, inputs, scores, actions, delayed outcomes, and calibration. A shifted input distribution is a warning to investigate, while a stable-looking input distribution cannot prove the concept remains unchanged.

sourceAnchor.heading: 9. Metrics, Calibration, Thresholds, and Subgroup Behavior
sourceAnchor.quote: **Calibration** asks whether events assigned probability near `p` occur about fraction `p` in the relevant population.

activities.prompt: A calibrated risk score feeds a team that can review only 500 cases per day. Which next step respects the complete decision system?

options.text: Evaluate a top-500 policy with real error costs, subgroup behavior, and an operational fallback
Use 0.5 because every calibrated score requires that threshold
Treat strong ranking as proof that the probabilities are calibrated
Stop measuring outcomes because offline evaluation already fixed the system

explanation.text: Review capacity makes top-k selection part of the policy. It must be evaluated with consequences and monitoring; the score alone neither chooses the threshold nor guarantees continued usefulness.

sourceAnchor.heading: 9. Metrics, Calibration, Thresholds, and Subgroup Behavior
sourceAnchor.quote: The model score is an input to policy, not the policy itself.
